title: Elihu Says God Speaks Through Pain
overview: Elihu, a younger man who has been listening, speaks directly to Job and argues that God does speak to people, through dreams and even through suffering, to turn them back from death.

parts.label: Elihu asks Job to listen (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: Elihu promises to speak honestly and says that he, like Job, was made by God out of clay, so Job has no reason to be afraid of him. Job had earlier wished he could argue his case with someone who would not overwhelm him, and Elihu seems to offer himself as that person.

parts.label: Job's complaint quoted back (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Elihu sums up what he heard Job say: that he is innocent, yet God treats him like an enemy and watches his every step like a prisoner in chains. Job had spoken this way in his anguish, though he never claimed to be completely without sin, so Elihu's summary is a little sharper than Job's actual words.

parts.label: God warns through dreams (vv. 12-18)
parts.note: Elihu says Job is wrong to claim God never answers, because God is greater than any person and speaks in more than one way, even if people miss it. One way is through frightening dreams at night, meant to pull someone back from pride and from the pit, meaning the grave.

parts.label: God warns through illness (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: A second way is sickness: a person in bed with aching bones, no appetite, and a body wasting away until they are close to death. Elihu treats this pain as a warning meant to rescue the person, an idea Eliphaz had touched on earlier, but Elihu spells it out at length.

parts.label: A messenger and a ransom (vv. 23-30)
parts.note: Elihu pictures a rare go-between, perhaps an angel, who speaks up for the dying person and says a ransom (a price that sets someone free) has been found, so the person is healed, prays, and gladly admits their wrongs to others. Scholars are unsure who this messenger is meant to be, and Christians have traditionally read the ransom as pointing to Jesus.

parts.label: An invitation to reply (vv. 31-33)
parts.note: Elihu tells Job to answer if he can and says he actually wants to clear Job's name. If Job has nothing to say, Elihu asks him to stay quiet and listen.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Elihu is a wise voice preparing the way for God's own speech or just another overconfident speaker, since God later rebukes Job's three friends but never mentions Elihu at all.
think: When you have gone through something painful, did it seem to carry any meaning or lesson, or was it simply pain?
